kikuyu: Kamũingĩ koyaga ndĩrĩ.
translation: A small group of people lifts the heavy wooden mortar.
explanation: Collective effort makes even the heaviest burden light. Attested in Marion S. Stevenson (1927) 'Specimens of Kikuyu Proverbs' (Festschrift Meinhof, p. 242) and Wiktionary.
englishEquivalent: Many hands make light work.

kikuyu: Kĩara kĩmwe gĩtiũragaga ndaa.
translation: One finger cannot kill (crush) a louse.
explanation: A single person acting alone cannot accomplish what requires community cooperation. Shared across Central Kenya Bantu (cf. Kamba 'Kĩaa kĩmwe kĩtiũaa ndaa', Lindblom 1920).
englishEquivalent: No man is an island / Two heads are better than one.

kikuyu: Rũtungu rũmwe rũtiraragia mwaki.
translation: One log alone does not keep the fire burning through the night.
explanation: In the traditional homestead hearth (riiko), three logs or hearthstones must meet to sustain a fire; likewise, a community or family depends on mutual support.
englishEquivalent: United we stand, divided we fall.

kikuyu: Rwambo rũmwe rũtiambaga ndarwa.
translation: A single peg cannot stretch out an animal hide.
explanation: Stretching and drying a cowhide requires many wooden pegs around its perimeter; a complex undertaking requires many contributors.
englishEquivalent: It takes a village.

kikuyu: Thegere igĩrĩ itiremagwo nĩ mwatũ.
translation: Two honey badgers are not defeated by a beehive.
explanation: When partners work together with determination, no obstacle or high beehive is beyond their reach.
englishEquivalent: Union is strength.

kikuyu: Ũũgĩ wa mũndũ ũmwe ndũrĩmaga.
translation: The wisdom of one person alone does not cultivate a field.
explanation: True wisdom is shared and tested in council (kiama, Hobley 1922 & Routledge 1910) rather than hoarded by one individual.
englishEquivalent: In the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

kikuyu: Ng'aragu ndĩhoyagwo ũhoro.
translation: One does not ask for news from a hungry person (or: Hunger is not interrogated).
explanation: Hospitality comes before interrogation: when a guest or traveller arrives, offer food and rest first before asking them to recount their journey (Stevenson 1927 / Wiktionary).
englishEquivalent: A hungry belly has no ears.

kikuyu: Wega uumaga na mũciĩ.
translation: Goodness (generosity and good character) begins at home.
explanation: Kindness, integrity, and care for others are first cultivated within one's own homestead (mũciĩ) before extending outward (Wiktionary).
englishEquivalent: Charity begins at home.

kikuyu: Mũceera na mũkũndũ akũndũkaga taguo.
translation: Whoever walks with a corrupt/tainted person becomes tainted like them.
explanation: A person's habits and reputation are shaped by the company they keep (Wiktionary).
englishEquivalent: Birds of a feather flock together / Bad company corrupts good character.

kikuyu: Kũhũra maaĩ na ndĩrĩ.
translation: To pound water in a mortar.
explanation: Classical Gĩkũyũ idiom for engaging in futile, unproductive labour (Wiktionary).
englishEquivalent: To beat the air / A fool's errand.

kikuyu: Ta gĩkwa na mũkũngũgũ.
translation: Like the yam vine and the mũkũngũgũ support tree.
explanation: Describes two inseparable friends or partners whose lives and livelihoods are intertwined like a yam vine climbing its support tree (Wiktionary & Routledge 1910, p. 371).
englishEquivalent: Inseparable companions / Thick as thieves.

kikuyu: Gũtirĩ mũthenya ũkĩaga ta ũrĩa ũngĩ.
translation: No day dawns exactly like another.
explanation: Times and circumstances constantly change; both hardship and prosperity require adaptability and patience (Stevenson 1927).
englishEquivalent: Every day brings its own dawn.

kikuyu: Mũndũ mũgo ndagũragĩra.
translation: A medicine man (mũndũ mũgo) does not divine for himself.
explanation: Even an expert or elder needs the objective counsel of others when facing personal trials (cf. W. S. & K. Routledge 1910, pp. 249–272 & Hobley 1922 on Mun'-du Mu-gu).
englishEquivalent: A physician cannot heal himself.

kikuyu: Mwana mũũgĩ nĩ ũrĩa ũiguaga kĩrĩra.
translation: A wise child is the one who listens to counsel and instruction.
explanation: Listening to elders' traditional instruction (kĩrĩra) is the foundation of wisdom (Stevenson 1927).
englishEquivalent: A wise son hears his father's instruction.

kikuyu: Kũmenya werũ nĩ kũũtinda.
translation: To know the open plain is to spend the day in it (from Hinde 1904 gu-tinda 'to spend the day').
explanation: True mastery of a place, craft, or people comes only from direct, patient experience.
englishEquivalent: Experience is the best teacher.

kikuyu: Mũgeni nĩ rũũĩ.
translation: A guest is like a river.
explanation: A visitor passes through briefly like flowing river water and should be welcomed generously while present (Stevenson 1927).
englishEquivalent: Welcome the coming, speed the parting guest.

kikuyu: Ki-nyan'-ga kya-ku a-ki-ni'-na ma-ru'-tu! (Wamahu's Ku-i-ne-né-ra Song, Routledge 1910, p. 185)
translation: Your little market has finished the banana trees! — Wait until we have finished dancing, and then I will tell you what I have in my heart.
explanation: Recorded verbatim by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, pp. 184–185) from Wamahu (brother of Chief Wombúgu on the Gúra River) on the Ku-i-ne-né-ra dance of warriors and young women.
englishEquivalent: First the communal dance, then the words of the heart.

kikuyu: O N'gaí! Mwi-nin-ya-ga! Give us health, give us children, give us rich increase of our flocks and herds and of the fruits of the earth! (Chief Mungé's Prayer, Routledge 1910, p. 231)
translation: O N'gaí (God)! Mwi-nin-ya-ga (Possessor of Whiteness on Mount Kénya)! Give us health, children, and increase of flocks, herds, and crops!
explanation: Recorded verbatim onto the phonograph by Chief Mungé for W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, pp. 230–231) during the sacrifice beneath the sacred Mu-gú-mu fig tree with eight sacrificial shrubs.
englishEquivalent: Health, posterity, and the fruits of the earth are the blessings of peace.

kikuyu: N'ga-na! — Sa-i! Sa-i! (Sacrificial Beer Responses, Routledge 1910, pp. 235–236)
translation: N'ga-na! ('So be it / Amen!') — Sa-i! Sa-i! ('Hear, hear!')
explanation: Recorded verbatim by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, pp. 235–236): the elders' antiphonal responses on the third day after the Mu-gú-mu sacrifice when four officiating elders pour sacrificial sugar-cane beer (n'jó-hi) at the foot of the sacred tree.
englishEquivalent: Let all the assembly say Amen.

kikuyu: Ta-hí-ka thá-hu! Ta-hí-ka ki-ú-ru! Ni-da-ni-na thá-hu wa-ku. (Routledge 1910, pp. 262–263)
translation: Vomit the ceremonial uncleanness (thá-hu)! Expel what is bad (ki-ú-ru)! I have ended your ceremonial uncleanness.
explanation: Recorded verbatim by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, pp. 260–263): spoken by the Medicine-Man (Mun'-du Mu-gu) while brushing the patient's lips from left to right with a brush of nine Tuso purification herbs and gon'-du, u'-mu, and í-ra diatomite.
englishEquivalent: Cast out the wrong and be restored to purity.

kikuyu: Wanjíru (Ro-gá-nu #2, Routledge 1910, pp. 291–293): The Maiden Sacrificed for Rain & Rescued by True Loyalty
translation: When severe drought parched the land, the Medicine-Man declared that the maiden Wanjíru must stand in the circle while each family gave a goat for her life; as she sank step by step into the earth, torrential rain fell, until a young warrior who loved her followed her track into the underworld ('a land of great plains') and restored her to her mother and sister.
explanation: Recorded verbatim from the storyteller Na-ga-tú-u by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, Part IV: Folk-Lore, pp. 291–293).
englishEquivalent: True devotion braves the underworld to rescue the innocent.

kikuyu: Thahu wa mũciĩ ũhoragio na ng'ondu (kũhoria thahu).
translation: Ceremonial defilement (thahu) of the homestead is cooled and purified with a sacrificial sheep (ng'ondu).
explanation: Documented in W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, pp. 256–263, 29 causes of Thá-hu) and C. W. Hobley (1910, pp. 134–141): peace and moral order in the homestead require ritual reconciliation ('cooling').
englishEquivalent: Prevention and reconciliation restore peace.

kikuyu: Kiama kia atumia gĩtũũragia bũrũri na thayũ.
translation: The council of elders (Kiama) sustains the land in peace.
explanation: Documented by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge in 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa' (1910, pp. 195–221: Mo-ran'-ja / N'dun'-du / Ke-thi-ga, Ki-á-ma with Ma-tu-ra N'gu-ru leaf-bunch and staff of Mu-ti'-gi, Mun'-deren'-du or Mú-ta-zi, N'já-ma, 9 dated court trials, 6 Mu-ma ordeals, and 14-hole Ki-tha-si stone) and Rev. Fr. A. Hémery (1903).
englishEquivalent: Where there is wise counsel, the people flourish.

kikuyu: Mũndũ ũtarĩ mbũri ndarĩ mũciĩ (Hémery 1903 & Routledge 1910).
translation: A person who does not care for their flock does not build a lasting homestead (fixed ratio: 13 goats = 1 cow, Routledge 1910, p. 44).
explanation: Grounded in Rev. Fr. A. Hémery's 'English-Kikuyu Handbook' (1903), McGregor (1904), and W. S. & K. Routledge (1910, pp. 44, 124–133, where bride-wealth marli is 30 goats and 5–6 sheep).
englishEquivalent: Diligence builds the home.

kikuyu: Gũthũ (Guso)! — Aanake mathiĩ, athuri maikare? — Mũhu ũitwo, mahiga ma riiko matigare.
translation: Riddle (Do you hear)! — The young men go, the old men stay? — Answer: The ashes are poured out, the three hearth-stones remain.
explanation: Recorded by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910, 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa', p. 192, Riddle #4): Kikuyu riddles open with 'Guso!' ('Do you hear?'). Just as hot ashes are swept out while the three hearthstones (mahiga ma riiko) stay fixed, young warriors travel afar while the elders (kiama) remain at the homestead.
englishEquivalent: Youth wanders, age endures.

kikuyu: Gũthũ (Guso)! — Kĩĩ kĩnyingĩtie? — Marigũ.
translation: Riddle (Do you hear)! — What hangs down? — Answer: Bananas (marigũ).
explanation: Recorded by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910, 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa', pp. 191–192, Riddle #1): Traditional Kikuyu 'Guso' riddle reflecting the heavy banana bunches hanging in every homestead plantation (mũgũnda).
englishEquivalent: Bountiful harvest bows low.

kikuyu: Gũthũ (Guso)! — Nĩkĩ ndĩraigua inegene? — Nyoni irĩ mũgũnda.
translation: Riddle (Do you hear)! — Why do I hear a noise? — Answer: The birds are in the plantation (shamba).
explanation: Recorded by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910, 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa', p. 192, Riddle #2): Refers to the commotion of grain-eating birds in the millet and maize fields, guarded by children on watch-platforms using the 26-in. bull-roarer (ke-hu-ru'-ta, Plate XXXII Fig. 1) and bark-twine mud-pellet sling (ki-gu'-tha, Plate XXXII Fig. 2).
englishEquivalent: Where there is commotion, there is a cause.

kikuyu: Gũthũ (Guso)! — Kĩĩ kĩgonderera njĩra-inĩ? — Ndorobo njĩra-inĩ.
translation: Riddle (Do you hear)! — What takes a winding course? — Answer: A forest hunter (N'doróbo / A'si) on the road.
explanation: Recorded by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910, 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa', p. 192, Riddle #3): Describes the winding forest tracks of the A'si (A-ki-e-ki / N'doróbo) elephant hunters across Mount Kenya and the Aberdares (pp. 3–4).
englishEquivalent: The forest path winds.

kikuyu: Gũthũ (Guso)! — Kĩĩ kĩambata kĩrĩma gĩkinye kĩrĩma kĩngĩ? — Kũgũrũ.
translation: Riddle (Do you hear)! — What goes from hill to hill? — Answer: The human foot (kũgũrũ).
explanation: Recorded by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910, 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa', p. 192, Riddle #5): In the ridge-and-valley topography of Kikuyuland, the human foot crosses from ridge to ridge.
englishEquivalent: Step by step crosses the mountains.

kikuyu: Warĩire kĩĩ ira, ka-Ndorobo? — Ũthĩ (ou-thi), na ngĩkoma. Wahuurire ta rwĩgĩ? — Ta rwĩgĩ rũtarĩ mũting'oe.
translation: What did you eat yesterday, little N'doróbo? — Scraps of food (ou-thi), and went to sleep. Did you snatch up your food like a hawk? — Like a hawk that has lost its tail.
explanation: Recorded verbatim by W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910, 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa', p. 192): Traditional Kikuyu boys' rapid-fire antiphonal wordplay game.
englishEquivalent: Quick wit parries every question.
